claims.text: The operative sentence is: "Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of Anthropic's shares will be committed today, with an additional 2% added at the board's discretion for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline."[^1]
The same post says the fund will be "a wholly-owned LLC—rather than a 501(c)(3) or other format", chosen for "adjustability between different forms of giving".[^1]
Reuters' wire story, the most first-hand independent account, adds no executive quotes and no figures, and confirms that the trigger sits "above a baseline that has yet to be disclosed".[^2]
Business Insider supplied the widely repeated "$48 billion", explicitly as arithmetic on "the company's most recent valuation in May".[^3]

It came four days after New York City's pension funds asked Anthropic to pause its IPO over governance,[^34] and in the same week Reuters reported that investors at Anthropic's investor day had discussed a valuation of about $1.5 trillion, against the roughly $2 trillion previously expected.[^9]

Delaware's §160(c) says a corporation's own shares held by an entity it controls "shall neither be entitled to vote nor be counted for quorum purposes", and it applies expressly to any entity "if a majority of the voting power of such other entity is held, directly or indirectly, by the corporation".[^13]

Under US GAAP, "shares of the parent held by a subsidiary shall not be treated as outstanding shares… [they] shall be eliminated in the consolidated financial statements and reflected as treasury shares."[^14]
A single-member LLC owned by a corporation is, by default, "reflected on its owner's federal tax return as a division of the corporation".[^15]

Crucially, nothing comparable to the private-foundation payout rule applies: a private foundation must distribute roughly 5% of its non-charitable assets each year or pay a 30% excise tax on the shortfall.[^16]
The ~$1.4T secondary figure reflects scarce, mostly preferred or fund-interest blocks trading 3–5× oversubscribed,[^12] up from about $1.2T in July.[^58]

The comparison it invites is Tesla's 2025 CEO award: "12 tranches of 35,311,992 shares per tranche", 12% of the adjusted share count in total, "requiring $8.5 trillion market capitalization for the last tranche", with a preliminary fair value of $87.75B.[^23]
Reuters' account of the draft S-1 says the board has *also* promised Dario and Daniela Amodei more RSUs, some tied to retention and some to the IPO.[^11]
Forbes estimates each holds "just over 1.7%",[^24] which puts the seven at about 11.9% and their 80% pledge at about 9.5% of Anthropic.
Bloomberg's wealth index says each owns "less than 1%",[^25] which caps the pledge at under 5.6%.
Anthropic's careers page today offers "optional equity donation matching at a 1:1 ratio, up to 25% of your equity grant."[^27]
Earlier hires reportedly received a 3:1 match on pledges of up to 50% of their grants,[^29,28] so a full early pledge plus match equals twice the original grant in donated shares.
The Information reported, per secondary summaries, more than $660M of non-cash expense for matching stock between October 2025 and March 2026, excluded from adjusted operating profit.[^29,30]
Calcbench's CEO called that treatment "not common at all".[^30]
In January 2026 Amodei described 80% of the founders' "wealth",[^26] while the S-1 language reported by Reuters is 80% of "personal Anthropic equity".[^11]
A widely cited LessWrong post says "apparently this pledge is not legally binding",[^28] and Forbes notes "it's not yet clear how, when or to where they will transfer any funds."[^24]
With Vas Narasimhan's appointment on 14 April 2026, "Trust-appointed directors now make up a majority of the Board", a board of seven that includes Dario and Daniela Amodei.[^32]
In August 2026 trustee Tino Cuéllar "stepped down from the Trust to join the company" as Chief Global Affairs Officer, running policy and government relations.[^33]
while Anthropic itself has given $40M to Public First Action, a 501(c)(4) AI-policy group.[^38]

According to Reuters' reading of the draft S-1, "a majority vote of the seven co-founders will direct a single share of Class F stock" amounting to "50.1% of the total voting power over key corporate matters", while the Trust elects the other four directors.[^10]
A gap between control and accountability is especially concerning for investors.

Delaware's PBC statute supplies one accountability tool, a stockholder benefit statement "no less than biennially", and limits suits to enforce the balancing duty to holders of 2% of shares (or $2M of listed shares).[^19]
Court filings in the Google search case showed Google owned 14% of Anthropic "but holds no voting rights, board seats, or board observer rights."[^37]
Google then committed $10B in cash at a $350B valuation in April 2026, with $30B more if performance targets are met.[^59]
That $200M is a research fund that "primarily fund[s] projects in the $5-30 million range", with "longer-duration unconditional income pilots at livable levels" on its agenda.[^39]
On those numbers, a 5% payout would equal about 6.5% of one ordinary year of US unemployment insurance, which was $36.9B in 2025 and $314.2B at the 2021 pandemic peak.[^42]

Against private philanthropy it is large: about 27% of the Gates Foundation's planned annual spend under its plan to give away $200B by 2045,[^44] about ten times GiveDirectly's annual transfers (over $1 billion delivered since 2009),[^43] and about 2% of the $109.81B US foundations gave in 2024 out of $592.50B total giving.[^45]

Its foundation holds a 26% stake "valued at approximately $130 billion",[^48] plus a warrant for "an undisclosed amount of additional shares" if OpenAI Group's share price "grows more than tenfold after 15 years".[^47]
Payout is a weak point for both: the OpenAI Foundation pledged $25B "without providing a time frame" and had granted $40.5M by December 2025.[^49]

On Hacker News one commenter wrote that the money goes "to an LLC that is owned and controlled by anthropic… that's the public good as decided by anthropic, not the public", and another called "a 2% for every 50% increase… just insulting."[^57]
